drafts.title: Maintain the distinctive exterior styling while offering visible personalization including an optional panoramic glass roof
drafts.description: Customers experience the 5 Series as a car that draws compliments and attention for its sporty-luxury exterior, while buyers who want variation can choose visible personalization (additional color/trim choices and an optional panoramic glass roof) at order.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At launch, >=75% of surveyed buyers rate exterior styling in the top-2 satisfaction tiers; the model lineup offers at least 3 additional exterior color/trim personalization choices and a factory-available panoramic glass roof option.
assumptions: Customer survey sample represents U.S. buyers (n ≥ 200) and uses the same top-2 satisfaction metric as existing studies.
Panoramic roof can be offered as a factory option without changing the car's overall packaging or crash structure.
uncertainties: Some customers want exterior changes that conflict with the current distinctive look; personalization choices must avoid diluting the core design appeal.

drafts.title: Keep the luxurious interior look and increase personalization including ambient lighting presets
drafts.description: Customers continue to experience a refined, easy-to-keep interior while gaining more personalization options (material/trim packages and ambient lighting presets) so those who reported unmet needs can tune the cabin to their taste.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At launch, >=80% of surveyed buyers rate interior design in the top-2 satisfaction tiers; ambient lighting provides at least 6 color presets and 4 intensity levels and, in a 100-customer evaluation, >=70% rate the ambient lighting options as 'satisfactory' or better.
assumptions: Customer survey sample (n ≥ 200) uses comparable top-2 satisfaction metric.
Lighting hardware and software personalization are implemented with noticeable distinctions between presets.
uncertainties: Individual tastes in materials and colors vary widely; offered packages must balance common preferences and premium positioning.

drafts.title: Seats remain highly comfortable and become more adjustable for shorter and smaller occupants
drafts.description: Customers experience seats that retain current comfort/support strengths while enabling shorter/smaller drivers to gain a better forward view and smaller occupants to avoid excessive bolstering or pressure.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a 30-person ergonomic study spanning 5th-percentile female to 95th-percentile male participants, >=95% can achieve a clear forward sightline over the hood to the first road marker (test condition) and >=90% rate seat comfort/support as 'satisfactory' or better; seats offer at least 5 distinct firmness/comfort settings and bolsters that are adjustable or tunable so that 90% of participants report bolsters neither pressing nor failing to support.
assumptions: Ergonomic study uses standard sightline test to an agreed road marker and includes representative occupant clothing/footwear.
Seat hardware provides the physical adjustment range to meet participant outcomes (this is an engineering detail; the requirement focuses on customer outcome).
uncertainties: Some extremes of occupant body shapes may still require special seating options or adjustments beyond defaults.

drafts.title: Access systems work reliably: all-doors default unlock and hands-free trunk opens consistently for users with hands full
drafts.description: Customers approaching the car with the key experience intuitive, predictable access: all doors unlock by default on approach (configurable) and the hands-free kick-to-open trunk works reliably with a single natural motion while carrying items.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Default out-of-box behavior unlocks all doors on approach; in 50 approach tests with typical user pockets/key fobs, ≥98% of tests unlock all doors as expected; hands-free trunk achieves ≥95% success within two attempts in 100 real-world trials (users carrying grocery-bag or similar items) and unintended trunk openings occur in ≤1% of 1000 parked checks.
assumptions: Tests use representative keys/key fobs and users perform motions typical of reported complaints.
Customers can change unlock behavior via a clearly discoverable setting in the vehicle UI.
uncertainties: Environmental factors (heavy rain, snow on bumper) may still reduce hands-free trunk reliability; acceptable thresholds assume normal conditions.

drafts.title: HVAC controls and vents are obvious and operable quickly, and interior storage is functionally usable
drafts.description: Customers can see and aim vents easily, adjust primary climate controls quickly without deep menu navigation, and find accessible storage for common items without searching.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a driving usability test, ≥90% of participants can locate and change driver temperature and fan speed within 5 seconds without more than a 2-second glance away from the forward view; vents are visible and can be aimed from the driver's seating position; at least one easily reachable storage compartment accommodates a common carry-on backpack (approx. 30 x 40 x 20 cm) and in a 100-customer evaluation ≥80% rate interior storage as 'satisfactory' or better.
assumptions: Driving usability test uses standardized tasks and participants representing typical U.S. drivers.
Storage acceptance uses commonly available backpack dimensions as a practical proxy for everyday cargo.
uncertainties: Some specialized items may still not fit; the requirement targets everyday convenience, not every possible cargo configuration.

drafts.title: Make flat-tire preparedness clear and accessible
drafts.description: Customers find the car's flat-tire preparedness easy to use and understand (spare, run-flat info or repair kit and how to use it) so they don't feel unprepared.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At launch the vehicle includes either an accessible spare tire or a trunk-located tire repair kit and clear trunk labeling; in a 200-customer survey, ≥80% of respondents rate flat-tire preparedness as 'satisfactory' or better.
assumptions: Customer survey (n ≥ 200) reflects U.S. buyer expectations for preparedness.
Choice between spare and repair kit is acceptable to customers if clearly communicated and accessible.
uncertainties: Some customers prefer a full-size spare while others accept repair kits; offering both is a cost/packaging trade-off.

drafts.title: Offer personalized cabin wellness and software-driven climate profiles to demonstrably improve perceived comfort (trial for next generation)
drafts.description: In next-generation customer trials, occupants experience measurable improvement in comfort on longer trips by using personalized climate and air-quality profiles managed by the vehicle software.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a 20-customer, two-week in-vehicle trial with personalized climate/air-quality profiles enabled versus baseline, ≥70% of participants report a measurable improvement in perceived comfort on long drives (self-reported comfort scale) and average in-cabin air-quality indicators (PM2.5 or VOC proxies) show improvement vs baseline during the trial.
assumptions: By launch (3–5 years) robust in-cabin sensors (air quality, temperature) and software personalization are available and allowed for production use.
Customer consent and data-privacy controls for any biometric or profile data are implemented.
Trial metrics rely on subjective comfort surveys plus sensor proxies for air quality (no regulatory approvals required to use such sensors).
uncertainties: Effectiveness depends on sensor accuracy, occupant acceptance of automated adjustments, and privacy regulations that may limit biometric data use.

drafts.title: Deliver a software-defined cockpit trial: large integrated HMI reduces control distraction for primary cabin tasks (next-generation bet)
drafts.description: Customers using a next-generation HMI experience faster, less distracting access to primary climate and comfort controls through a combination of larger integrated displays, simpler menus and persistent quick-controls, reducing time looking away from the road.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a user trial comparing current layout to the new cockpit, ≥85% of participants can change primary climate settings (temperature or fan level) within 2 taps or a single glance-and-tap and report lower perceived distraction; objective task time for these actions decreases by ≥40% versus the current model.
assumptions: Larger displays and redesigned HMI paradigms will be technically and legally feasible at launch and do not introduce new regulatory constraints.
Users accept software-driven controls if quick physical or persistent on-screen shortcuts remain available.
uncertainties: Some customers prefer tactile physical controls; the HMI must preserve low-effort access for primary functions to avoid alienating that group.
